prompt: `work_mem` showed `4MB`, yet it is not among the 25 active lines of Ubuntu's `postgresql.conf`. Where does the 4MB come from?
hint: What applies when no file sets a parameter?

choices.text: From the commented-out line `#work_mem = 4MB`
choices.why: A comment is ignored by the server. It documents the default; it does not set it.

choices.text: From a file in conf.d that the package installed
choices.why: The directory was empty: `ls -l` printed `total 0`.

choices.text: The default compiled into the PostgreSQL server
choices.why: Right. Any parameter no file sets keeps its built-in default.

choices.text: From postgresql.auto.conf in the data directory
choices.why: That file held only its two comment lines until ALTER SYSTEM wrote to it.

prompt: You add `shared_buffers = 512MB` to `conf.d/10-memory.conf`, while line 130 of `postgresql.conf` still says `128MB`. After a restart, which value does the server use?
hint: Where is `include_dir` in the main file, and which value wins?

choices.text: 128MB, because the main file outranks the files it includes
choices.why: There is no rank between files, only order. The include comes at the end, so it is read last.

choices.text: Neither: the server refuses to start with a parameter set twice
choices.why: A name set twice is allowed and silent. That is exactly why it is a hazard.

choices.text: 512MB
choices.why: Right. conf.d is read after the main file, and the last value read for a name wins.

choices.text: The smaller of the two, as a safety measure
choices.why: The server does not compare values. The later line simply replaces the earlier one.

prompt: In postgresql.conf, `shared_buffers = 128mb` is an error, because memory units are case-sensitive: the correct spelling is 128___.
hint: Megabytes, as the file's header spells it.

prompt: `pg_settings` shows `shared_buffers` with setting `16384` and unit `8kB`. How much memory is that?
hint: Multiply by the unit.

choices.text: 16 MB
choices.why: That reads 16384 as kilobytes. The unit is 8 kB pages.

choices.text: 128 MB
choices.why: Right: 16384 × 8 kB, the same value SHOW printed.
That ignores the unit column altogether.

choices.text: 8 GB
choices.why: That multiplies by 8 MB instead of 8 kB.

prompt: Match each `context` to what a new value takes before it applies.
hint: The column answers: what does it take to change this?

pairs.right: a SET in the session, by anybody
nothing will change it on this cluster

right_distractors: a new connection to the database, as a superuser

prompt: `data_directory` is written in `postgresql.conf`, yet `pg_settings` says its source is `override`. Why?
hint: Look at the command line in lesson 3's `ps` output.

choices.text: ALTER SYSTEM overrode it in postgresql.auto.conf
choices.why: A value from that file shows `configuration file` with the file's name as sourcefile.

choices.text: The server was started with `-D`, which sets it
choices.why: Right. The value comes from how the postmaster was started; the line in the file is a note.

choices.text: The line in the file has a syntax error and was skipped
choices.why: A skipped line would appear in pg_file_settings with an error, and the server would not have found its data.

choices.text: `override` is what every postmaster parameter shows
choices.why: `max_connections` is postmaster too and showed `configuration file`, line 65.

prompt: After a reload, the log ends with `configuration file ... contains errors; unaffected changes were applied`. The line above it says `parameter "shared_buffers" cannot be changed without restarting the server`. What is wrong with the file?
hint: Read the lines above the word errors.

choices.text: Nothing: one value is waiting for a restart
choices.why: Right. The file is valid; pending_restart is true for shared_buffers until the next restart.

choices.text: shared_buffers is misspelt
choices.why: A misspelt name produces `unrecognized configuration parameter`, a different line.

choices.text: The value 256MB exceeds what the machine allows
choices.why: The restart then applied it without complaint: 32768 pages of 8 kB.

choices.text: Every change in the file was rejected
choices.why: The log says the opposite: log_min_duration_statement changed at once.

prompt: A colleague put `work_mem = 64mb` in a conf.d file, reloaded, and saw no complaint from `systemctl`. The server is running normally. What is the risk?
hint: What does the server do with that file the next time it starts?

choices.text: None: a bad value is skipped and the default used, at reload and at start alike
choices.why: Only the reload forgives it. At start the same line is FATAL.

choices.text: The next restart fails
choices.why: Right. The running server kept 4MB, but at start it refuses a file with an invalid value.

choices.text: Every session is now using 64 kilobytes of work_mem
choices.why: The value was refused, not reinterpreted: SHOW work_mem still printed 4MB.

choices.text: Connections opened after the reload are refused
choices.why: New connections work; the bad line affects nothing until the server reads the files at start.

prompt: Which of these cuts every open connection?
hint: One rereads the files; one stops the server.

choices.text: `SELECT pg_reload_conf();`
choices.why: That sends SIGHUP; sessions stay connected and receive the new values.

choices.text: `sudo systemctl reload postgresql`
choices.why: A reload, the same signal as pg_reload_conf().

choices.text: `sudo pg_ctlcluster 16 main reload`
choices.why: Ubuntu's wrapper for the same reload.

choices.text: `sudo systemctl restart postgresql`
choices.why: Right. A restart stops the server, so every session and transaction ends.

prompt: You set `work_mem = 8MB` in conf.d and reload, and SHOW still prints 16MB. `pg_file_settings` shows your line with `applied = f`. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: Which file does the server read last?

choices.text: work_mem needs a restart, not a reload
choices.why: work_mem is a user parameter; a reload applies it.

choices.text: The conf.d file is not named in postgresql.conf
choices.why: include_dir reads every .conf file in the directory; the line was read, it appears in pg_file_settings.

choices.text: 8MB is below the minimum for work_mem
choices.why: The minimum is 64 kB, and an invalid value shows an error rather than applied = f alone.

choices.text: Somebody ran ALTER SYSTEM SET work_mem = '16MB'
choices.why: Right. postgresql.auto.conf is read after conf.d and wins.

prompt: Put these layers in the order the server applies them, the first applied at the top; the last one to set a value wins.
hint: Files first, in the order they are read; then what belongs to the connection.
trap: ALTER SYSTEM's file comes after conf.d, not before it.

prompt: `ALTER SYSTEM SET work_mem = '64mb';` answered with an error, where the same typo in a conf.d file was accepted until the reload. Why the difference?
hint: Who reads the value at the moment it is written?

choices.text: ALTER SYSTEM applies the value immediately, so it must be valid
choices.why: It applies nothing: the 16MB took effect only after pg_reload_conf().

choices.text: ALTER SYSTEM only accepts values in kilobytes
choices.why: '16MB' was accepted in the next statement.

choices.text: ana is not allowed to change work_mem with ALTER SYSTEM
choices.why: ana is a superuser, and the error named the value, not a permission.

choices.text: It checks the value before writing a line
choices.why: Right. The server checks the value at once; an editor knows nothing about units.

prompt: A connection matches line 125 and fails its password check. Line 127 below would also admit it. What happens?
hint: Does the server keep reading after a match?

choices.text: The server tries line 127 next
choices.why: There is no falling through: the first matching line decides alone.

choices.text: It is admitted with a warning in the log
choices.why: A failed method is a FATAL refusal, with the reason in the log.

choices.text: It is refused
choices.why: Right. The first line that matches is the only one that counts.

choices.text: psql asks for the password a second time, as line 127
choices.why: psql's second attempt was with and without encryption, both against line 125.

prompt: Why does the client see only `password authentication failed`, when the log says `User "ana" has no password assigned`?
hint: Who should learn which roles exist?

choices.text: psql truncates long server messages
choices.why: psql printed the whole message; the server chose to send less.

choices.text: The DETAIL is written later, by a background process
choices.why: Both log lines carry the same timestamp and process id.

choices.text: The client gave up before the server could explain
choices.why: The server sent its FATAL and closed; the explanation is withheld on purpose.

choices.text: So a stranger learns nothing about which roles exist or have passwords
choices.why: Right. The detail is for the administrator who reads the log.

prompt: Match each pg_hba.conf method to what it does.
hint: One asks the kernel, one asks for a password, one admits, one refuses.

pairs.right: the operating-system user must match the role
a password, proved through a challenge

prompt: An application on 10.0.0.15 gets `FATAL: no pg_hba.conf entry for host "10.0.0.15", user "app", database "shop", no encryption`. What does that tell you?
hint: It got a FATAL from PostgreSQL, so it reached something.

choices.text: The server is not listening on that network
choices.why: Then the client would get Connection refused from the kernel and no FATAL at all.

choices.text: The password for app is wrong
choices.why: A wrong password needs a matching line first, and gives password authentication failed.

choices.text: The role app does not exist
choices.why: The file is checked before the role is looked up; the message names the file.

choices.text: It reached the server, and no line matches those four values
choices.why: Right. Listening works; a host line for that address, role and database is missing.

prompt: Which of these parameters should keep its default on every server you run?
hint: One of them protects the data against a power cut.

choices.text: fsync
choices.why: Right. Off, a power cut corrupts the cluster.

choices.text: shared_buffers
choices.why: Its default of 128MB is small for most servers; lesson 6 sizes it.

choices.text: listen_addresses
choices.why: Any server that serves another machine changes it.

choices.text: log_min_duration_statement
choices.why: Off by default, and lesson 19 turns it on.

prompt: After setting `listen_addresses = '*'` and reloading, `ss -ltn` still shows only `127.0.0.1:5432`. Why?
hint: Look at its context.

choices.text: pg_hba.conf has no line for other addresses
choices.why: pg_hba.conf decides who is admitted, not where the server listens.

choices.text: It is a postmaster parameter: it needs a restart
choices.why: Right. The sockets are opened at start; the restart in the lesson changed ss to 0.0.0.0.

choices.text: The firewall hides the other sockets from ss
choices.why: ss lists the machine's own listening sockets; a firewall filters packets, not that list.

choices.text: '*' is IPv6-only and ss -ltn shows IPv4
choices.why: '*' means every address; after the restart ss showed 0.0.0.0.

prompt: How many of the parameters in the course's table of the handful worth touching need a restart to change: listen_addresses, max_connections, shared_buffers, shared_preload_libraries, work_mem, max_wal_size?
hint: work_mem is user, max_wal_size is sighup.

prompt: You inherit a server and want to know, before anyone restarts it, whether a restart would change anything or fail. Which pair of checks answers both?
hint: One view knows what is waiting; one command reads the files as a start would.

choices.text: SHOW all, and systemctl status
choices.why: Both describe the running server; neither reads the files as a restart will.

choices.text: grep on postgresql.conf, and pg_lsclusters
choices.why: grep misses conf.d and postgresql.auto.conf, and pg_lsclusters says only online or down.

choices.text: A reload, then reading whether systemctl printed an error
choices.why: systemctl reload printed nothing even with the typo in place.

choices.text: pending_restart in pg_settings, and postgres -C on the files
choices.why: Right. The first lists changes not yet applied; the second fails exactly where a start would.

prompt: You add `host shop app 10.0.0.15/32 scram-sha-256` at the bottom of pg_hba.conf, below a line `host all all 10.0.0.0/24 reject`, and reload. What does app on 10.0.0.15 get?
hint: Which line does the connection meet first?

choices.text: A password prompt, since its own line is more specific
choices.why: Specificity counts for nothing; order decides, and the reject line comes first.

choices.text: no pg_hba.conf entry
choices.why: Two lines match; the message would be pg_hba.conf rejects connection.

choices.text: Refused by the reject line
choices.why: Right. 10.0.0.15 is inside 10.0.0.0/24, so the earlier line decides. Move the new line above it.

choices.text: The reload fails because the two lines contradict each other
choices.why: Overlapping lines are normal and legal; only order separates them.

prompt: Match each symptom to the change that is missing.
hint: Kernel, file, method, restart.

pairs.right: listen_addresses does not include that address
a host line for that client
a correct password for the role

prompt: A report needs `work_mem = 256MB`, and only the role `reporting` runs it. Which change gives it that without touching anybody else?
hint: There is a layer per role.

choices.text: ALTER SYSTEM SET work_mem = '256MB', then a reload
choices.why: That gives every connection 256MB per sort, which lesson 6 shows is how a machine runs out of memory.

choices.text: work_mem = 256MB in conf.d/50-reporting.conf
choices.why: A file in conf.d applies to the whole server, whatever its name says.

choices.text: ALTER DATABASE shop SET work_mem = '256MB'
choices.why: Every role connecting to shop would get it, not just reporting.

choices.text: ALTER ROLE reporting SET work_mem = '256MB'
choices.why: Right. It applies from that role's next connection, and to nobody else.

prompt: The view that lists every line of every configuration file in the order read, with `applied` and `error` columns, is pg___.
hint: Not pg_settings: that one shows the values in use.
